text:
Both policies answer the same question: when a CPU writes to an address that’s in the cache, when does main memory find out?

Write-through

On every write, the cache updates its own copy and immediately writes the value to the next level (memory or a lower cache). Memory is always consistent with the cache.

Pros: Simple. Memory is never stale, so cache coherence in multiprocessor systems is easier, and a cache line can be dropped on eviction without writing anything back. Crash recovery is easier because memory holds the latest data.
Cons: Every store generates memory traffic, so write bandwidth and latency become a bottleneck. This is usually softened with a write buffer, which lets the CPU continue while writes drain in the background, but the buffer can still fill under heavy write bursts.

Write-back

On a write hit, the cache updates only its own copy and sets a dirty bit on that line. Memory is updated later, when the dirty line is evicted (or flushed explicitly).

Pros: Repeated writes to the same line collapse into a single memory write, which saves a lot of bandwidth and power. Writes complete at cache speed. It also lets you write whole lines in bursts, which memory handles efficiently.
Cons: More complex. You need dirty bits and eviction logic, and evicting a dirty line costs an extra write that can add latency on a miss. Memory can hold stale data, so multiprocessor systems need a coherence protocol (MESI and similar) to make sure other cores and DMA devices see the right values. A crash or power loss can lose data that was only in the cache.

Write misses: the second decision

A cache line is the unit of data storage in the cache. When a write misses the cache, the controller must decide whether to fetch the block from memory or bypass the cache entirely; these policies are mutually dependent with the write policies as they determine the data flow efficiency.

Each policy is usually paired with a write-miss policy:

Write-allocate loads the line into the cache, then performs the write. This is typically paired with write-back, since later writes to nearby data will then hit.
No-write-allocate sends the write straight to memory without loading the line. This is typically paired with write-through, since there’s little benefit in caching data you only wrote.

Summary

	Write-through	Write-back
Memory traffic	High (every write)	Low (on eviction)
Memory consistency	Always up to date	Can be stale
Complexity	Low	Higher (dirty bits, coherence)
Eviction cost	None	Extra write if dirty
Data-loss risk on crash	Low	Higher

In practice: Write-back dominates in modern CPU caches (L1 through L3) because bandwidth and speed matter most. Write-through shows up where consistency and simplicity matter more, such as some L1 designs (often paired with a write-back L2 behind them), embedded systems, and storage or database layers that need durability guarantees. The same tradeoff appears outside hardware too: OS page caches and disk controllers use write-back for speed, while “write-through” modes are offered when you can’t afford to lose recent writes.

analysis.main_topic: Write-through and write-back cache update policies and their tradeoffs.
primary_claims: Write-through keeps memory consistent with the cache by updating both on every write, while write-back only updates the cache and defers memory updates until eviction.
Write-through is simpler and easier for cache coherence but incurs higher memory traffic/latency.
Write-back improves performance by collapsing repeated writes and completing at cache speed, but adds complexity and data loss risk.
Write-miss policies like write-allocate and no-write-allocate are typically paired with write-back and write-through respectively.
Write-back is the dominant policy in modern CPU caches, whereas write-through is reserved for scenarios requiring high consistency or durability.
missing_intermediate_steps: Details on how specific coherence protocols like MESI actually resolve the staleness in write-back systems.
Explanation of the mechanics of a write buffer.
assumed_prior_knowledge: General understanding of computer memory hierarchy levels.
The basic concept of what a CPU cache is.
Basic awareness of what cache eviction is.
possible_confusions: Confusing the write policy (how data is written) with the write-miss policy (what to do on a cache miss).
Assuming write-through is always worse due to memory traffic, ignoring its role in simplified coherence.
ambiguous_references: The in 'the buffer can still fill' (referring to the write buffer mentioned previously).
Other cores in 'make sure other cores... see the right values' (implied CPU cores).

learning_objectives: Distinguish between write-through and write-back cache policies
Identify the performance and consistency tradeoffs of each policy
Understand the association between write-miss policies and write strategies
Identify real-world scenarios where each policy is preferred
prerequisite_order: Understanding of memory hierarchy (cache vs RAM)
Basic knowledge of computer architecture performance bottlenecks
explanation_sequence: Define the core goal of cache update policies
Explain Write-through mechanism and its simplicity/consistency benefits
Explain Write-back mechanism and its performance/bandwidth benefits
Contrast the two using a summary of pros/cons
Define Write-allocate vs No-write-allocate to clarify miss handling
plan.analogy_rationale: An analogy comparing a clerk writing in a shared logbook (Write-through) vs. writing on a personal sticky note that gets filed in the ledger at the end of the day (Write-back) helps conceptualize the consistency vs. latency tradeoff.
techniques_not_needed: Advanced technical proofs of cache coherence protocols, as it would overwhelm the fundamental comparison of the policies

preserved_claims: Write-through writes to the cache and the backing store before the write is considered complete.
Write-back writes to the cache first and copies the changed data to backing storage later.
Write-back can lose unflushed changes if the cache fails before writing back; write-through writes to backing storage more immediately.
Write-back usually has faster write performance because it delays the slower backing-store writes.
fidelity.notes: The rewrite added a definition for 'cache line' at the start of the 'Write misses' section, but this does not contradict or alter the original technical claims.
